utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. Happy new year. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Well, let me do the same. I wish you all a very good year and especially to the accused, the Defence counsel and the Prosecution. I hope that this year will be the best it can, given the circumstances, and my wishes go to your families, of course. I have a housekeeping announcement to do. There is going to be a trial, Trial number 7; therefore, the president of this Tribunal asked all the Trial Chamber to cancel a few hearings so that Trial number 7 can start. Therefore, regarding the Prlic case, it was decided that on the 18th of February - it's a Wednesday - and on the 26th of February - a Thursday - there will not be any Prlic hearing. I'm looking at the schedule for the Stojic Defence witnesses scheduled on those days. For the 18th of February, at first glance, it shouldn't be a problem because the witness is scheduled for three hours over four days, though, so we'll have three days. That can be done. As to the 26th of February, the witness scheduled was scheduled for two hours in examination-in-chief, so cancel -- the fact of cancelling the 26th should not be a major problem. This is what I wanted to tell you so that you can all make the necessary arrangements. I'm still having the schedule of witnesses for the Stojic Defence in front of me. Taking into account the number of hours allotted to the other Defence teams based on my empirical calculations - they're just indicative - unless something unforeseen happens, we should be able to finalise the Defence witnesses at the earliest in the week of May 2010. So this is the scheduling based on the hours allotted so far. I don't know if you are interested in this, but we should for the Stojic Defence finish around the 23rd of April. Thereafter, we'll have the Praljak Defence that will start, and the last Praljak Defence witnesses should testify end of August 2009. So we shall resume after the recess with the Petkovic witnesses of September 2009, to continue until early December 2009. And then we'll have the first Coric witnesses until March 2010, and we would start in the last week of March 2010 with Mr. Pusic witnesses, to continue and finish in May 2010. That is, of course, provided everything runs according to schedule as was suggested and provided all the hours are complied with as allotted by the Trial Chamber. So let's bet on May 2010 to hear the last witnesses. Mr. Registrar, can we move to private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in open session, we are going to have Mr. Prlic's witness, Mr. Cvikl, who is about to start his testimony. The Trial Chamber learned that this witness wanted to be able to use his laptop. The Trial Chamber discussed it and noticed that ever since the inception of this Tribunal, never did a witness come with his own laptop to testify. Therefore, the Trial Chamber is not in a position to grant the witness the use of his personal laptop. However, we believe that he wanted to have his laptop in order to refer to his report. But we have a written report, so it's easy enough. Mr. Cvikl can have in front of him his written report, and he can look at it and look at the footnotes in it. This is what I wanted to tell you as a preliminary observation. The Prlic Defence will need four hours; is that right, Mr. Karnavas? I greet you again with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom, and happy 2009. As I understand it, we will probably need four hours. We will try to do it in less than four hours. We do have a PowerPoint presentation. Just for a point of clarification, the use of laptop was only for a quick find of something, but -- that won't be a problem. But in any event, we do have a PowerPoint presentation. We provided hard copies to everyone as well as a table that goes with -- that has the documents that we will be referring to. We will endeavour to do it in less than four, but probably we will need four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Usher, can you have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope you can hear me. Please state your surname, first name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Milan Cvikl. My date of birth is May 19, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Currently I work as a general secretary and Chief of Staff of the government of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you had an opportunity to testify before a domestic or international court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my first time I'm going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated. Let me give you some explanation, but I believe that Mr. Karnavas has already explained that to you, but you never know. Given your high-ranking occupation or your functions in the past and today, I'm sure that you'll understand very quickly that these proceedings are proceedings in which the Judges are on the back line, as it were, because on the frontline you have questions put by parties, by the Defence and the Prosecution, started with Mr. Karnavas, based on the work you've done, following which the other Defence teams will ask questions of you, as well, as part of the so-called cross-examination. When this is over, the Prosecutor on your right-hand side will cross-examine you. But the four judges -- well, there are three today because one of us is ill, and I hope he'll return very soon, the Judges also have questions for you if need be based on the documents submitted to you. We know that there are a lot of documents to go through, and without further adieu, I shall ask Mr. Karnavas to proceed, of course, it being understood that you are now a witness of the Court so that in the next few days, because you are bound to testify over the whole week, you are not supposed to have any contact with Mr. Karnavas, but I think you've been told so by Mr. Karnavas in person. So this is what I had to tell you, and I very gladly ask Mr. Karnavas to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, for your testimony today, you prepared a PowerPoint preparation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I prepared a short PowerPoint presentation to summarize the report which has been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And because you're going to be speaking English and I speak English and because we have these terrific translators that do need some time to get it right, I would ask that you pause a little bit after hearing the question before answering.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay? Speak slowly and enunciate. That would help. Now, as I understand it, you did prepare a report, and that would be 1D 03111. Is that correct? Could we have it on the screen, or do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: I have that report with me in one of the binders, and it's the report which I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just a couple of questions on this report before we get into it. Who prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That report has been prepared by myself on the basis of the documents which were provided, many from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we were to turn to Roman numeral -- page Roman numeral vii, the preface portion of it, there we can find a section on your educational background and experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's a short CV of myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go on to the following page, which would be page Roman numeral viii, under the section "Object of the Analysis," and we continue on, we see more or less the tasks that you were assigned, the documents that you reviewed, and the individuals that you met with and spoke with in preparation for your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct. On these mentioned pages, there is, you know, what I have done, analyse the documents which were provided for me as far as the documents related to the socioeconomic finance key issues in the -- first, Croatian community, and then later, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and then for that I had been utilizing the documents provided. Plus, I have also identified some additional documents that explain what was happening on the economic front during the collapse of Yugoslavia and later on in different parts of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And, of course, we can look at the table of contents, which is on Roman numeral I, and it goes on, I believe, into Roman numeral III or IV, and very briefly, the PowerPoint presentation that you prepared for your testimony, can you please explain to us whether that indeed follows and is consistent with your report, or does it contain anything -- any material that is not in the report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: No. The PowerPoint presentation which I had prepared is based on the report. It is the presentation which summarize what is in the report and, of course, I wanted to summarize around 38 slides, the most important events for the Judges and for the -- all of you to understand the essence of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I also understand that along with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that along with this PowerPoint presentation, there are a list of documents somewhere in the neighbourhood of 40 or so, perhaps a few more. Are those -- are all those documents referenced in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Practically all of them are referenced in the report. A couple of them that I have been -- that were submitted to me later, which I could not include it in the report, but most of the documents, they are in the report and even additional documents, they are in -- basically just describing what has been happening and what I described in the report as presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who presented you with those documents, the additional ones that are not in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: The additional documents were presented to me by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That was over the last weekend when I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when we get to them, I would kindly ask you to point out that these are additional documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, they have been provided to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could turn to the PowerPoint presentation and get right into it. And basically, look at slide number 3. In here, in this slide you provide us a basic outline of your professional experience, and I would like to start with the bottom, with the very last one, that is, your current position. You indicated that you were the general secretary and Chief of Staff of the government of Slovenia. Could you please explain that position for us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. As of November 22nd, when the new Slovenian government, the Karnavan [phoen], met on its first session, as the first point of agenda of the first session on the proposal of the prime minister, the government had elected me as the general secretary or Chief of Staff of the government. It is the highest administration post in the Slovenian administration, and I work closely with the prime minister, but I have a team organised in the general Secretariat of the government, around 120 people directly under me and then some couple of hundred in different small departments. And we coordinate the work of the government, the three main bodies of the government, one to deal with the -- mainly what we will say economic issues; that one is shared by one of the ministers. Then there is the other one which deals with the state organisation and public affairs that is chaired by a Minister for Internal Affairs. Then there's the third body of the government, the so-called Body For Administration and Personnel Issues, which are chaired by myself. Government meet in this three committees, and then each Thursday morning at 10 o'clock there's the session of the government, and I under the guidance of the prime minister put together the agenda and then make sure that all the decisions of the government are prepared in according to the bylaws on how it should be done, and then also after the decision are made they are appropriately distributed to the country or to the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when you said November, the new government, this was November 2008?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, this is November 22nd, 2008. We had elections on 21st of September, 2008. I run these elections, and then we two months later got a new government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It's important that we have the time-frame so that we all know the period in which we're speaking of. Now, if we move from your current position and we move backwards, I see that you are also -- before this position, you were minister of the EU affairs in Slovenia. Could you please briefly describe that position.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. In the year 2004, just before we entered formally on May the 1st, 2004, to the European Union, I was appointed, elected in Slovene parliament as the minister of European affairs, where I worked as one of the members of the council of the ministers responsible for general affairs issue, and then I also coordinated the work of the ministers of Slovene government when they are dealing with European Union matters, and I represent the Slovene government in Slovene parliament when we are identifying the most important issues that we have to agree as far as the position of Slovenia is concerned in relation to the EU matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And prior to that, I understand from the first slide, you were a commercial banker, and if you could briefly describe that position as well as the one before that where you are the state secretary ministry of finance.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. In the period '98 to 2004, that's the period after I returned home from Washington where I was with the World Bank, I first was a team leader of an analytical research team in the Nova Ljubljanska banka, and later in 1998 I become the state secretary or a deputy minister of finance, if one can say so, for the public finance public expenditures management issues in Slovenia, which means I was responsible for preparation of the Slovene budgets, the central government budget as well as the budget of the other para-fiscal or para-budgetary funds, the health budget, the pension budget, and I was at that time also head of the negotiating team, which in period 1998, 2000 was negotiating with European Union issues of approval of the EU-related legislation in Slovenia environment as a part of Slovenia becoming a member of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to skip over your activities with the World Bank. We'll get to that. But first, if you could talk a little bit about the first bullet on frame 3 of your PowerPoint presentation when you are a macroeconomist. This would have been for Slovenia. If you could briefly discuss that position.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. I concluded my studies in 1983. The studies finished with my thesis on the issues of the -- mainly the so-called monetary supply money-demand issues in market economy, and I started to work as part of a team in, at that time, National Bank of Slovenia, which was part of the federal monetary system of the former Federation, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And in the period 1983 to 1991, in that team we have been very much following what was happening in Yugoslavia and what kind of reforms should have been undertaken for Yugoslavia to remain as an economically sustainable society. However, unfortunately, by late 1989 there was a hyperinflation. Early '99 [sic], there was reforms initiated by then -- last prime minister Mr. Markovic. Those reforms were not successful, and by the summer of 1990, I was appointed a member of a narrow team, which in the central bank and in other Slovene government institutions start with preparation for the independence of Slovenia. And as a part of that, I single-handedly wrote a couple of legislation, Bank of Slovenia Act, the New Central Bank of Slovenia Act, as well as calculated the amount of money that need to be printed in order to undertake the monetary transition once Slovenia become independent in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was done all prior to the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That was done all prior to the break-up of Yugoslavia. We have practically on the eve of the referendum, which was held on Slovenia on the 23rd of December, 1990, we had prepared in the central bank and in other government institutions legislation needed for Slovenia, first, of course, go for Slovene -- cities as to go to the referendum to make a decision whether they would want Slovenia to become independent country; and six months later, we had made arrangements, which, of course, created independent country, and I was part of that team up to early August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's briefly speak about your experience with the World Bank, and the reason I kept that last because as I understand it, it's in your report in your CV at some point with the World Bank you were in Bosnia Herzegovina. So briefly discuss your experience with the World Bank.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: I -- in late 1990, early 1991, I went on a concur [phoen] with the World Bank, the so-called young professional concur, where I was elected in a group of 30 young professionals that were employed with the World Bank in 1991. I started with two short 6-month assignments from September 1991 until September 1992, one in Tanzania and one in the industry and energy sector in the European department. And then in late -- second half of 1992 and 1993, I was an economist for the former Yugoslavia public of Macedonia. I led a team. I was a task manager, and that team prepared in the course of late 1992 and early 1993 the first economic recovery loan for Macedonia, for Former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia, where we, of course, ensured that Former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia would become member of the World Bank. In the summer of 1994, I was asked by then-director of the European department, Mr. Kamandervis [phoen], to form a small team of myself and the head of the World Bank, Rezda [phoen] mission in Warsaw to start establishing contacts with officials of, at that time, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina because we need to assure that -- after all other former Yugoslavia republics became member of the World Bank, we wanted to ensure that, also, the World Bank and the IMF would undertake necessary economic work for the -- for the Bosnia-Herzegovina to inherit the place of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the World Bank. And then I was there a part of the team which prepared the economic work. In 1995, we travelled extensively and have a lot of contacts with officials from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in early 1996, in February 1996, post-Dayton period, I also organised the first post-war reconstruction or international donors' conference in middle of Sarajevo, and then I continued to work on Bosnia-Herzegovina for another half a year or 9 months, and then in early 1997 I returned back home to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just very briefly, from that experience, I understand it was in 1994 that you went to Warsaw, your first trip into BiH was in 1995, and that you were in and out all the way to 1996. Did you draw any conclusions from that experience?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, the main conclusions which we draw at that time were summarized in this report, the Bosnia-Herzegovina toward economic recovery --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, hold on, because every time you refer to a report, we need to make sure that we are referring to a document, and I understand that this is 1D 02967; is that correct? If you look at your binder, which is --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so briefly discuss this particular report.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: This report was the first piece of economic work which the World Bank prepared. It was a World Bank country study, but it has two purposes: One, it was to present to the international community at large what were economic events after the war -- after the Yugoslavia ceased to exist, after the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we need to be sure in the World Bank that the unpaid or un -- current debt, which was at that time due from Bosnia-Herzegovina toward the World Bank, would be covered; and second, we work on this report together with International Monetary Fund and the EU institutions because we wanted to analyse, what are the post-war reconstruction needs of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that initially you were in Warsaw in 1994, and while you were there, were any one or any missions or any high-level personnel coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina to visit the World Bank officials that were there to -- for the purposes of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. We at that time were not able to travel into Bosnia-Herzegovina, what would be usually the way the World Bank does economic work. So we have asked authorities -- I met in September, October 1994 for the first time authorities from, at that time, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we have asked them to come to visit us in the Rezda mission of the World Bank, and then there was the World Bank team and authorities from Bosnia-Herzegovina where we exchanged opinions, and we also looked into the documents which they brought to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you recall some of the individuals that came on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina there, whether it be for the Federation or the state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yeah. A lot of them, for example, Mr. Enes Gotovusa, he was a high official of the Federal Secretariat for industry; Sefika Hacizowic

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Omicevic from the, at that time, National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina; Mr. Neven Tomic was also coming to visit us; Mr. Zlatko Bas [phoen], Mr. Petar Bosnic [phoen], a lot of officials, and they are actually mentioned, also, in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just very quickly, if we do look at this particular document, 1D 02967, on Roman numeral VII under "Acknowledgement," you know, we see several names including Mr. Tomic and Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Are these the names that you are referring to that either came to Warsaw or later had contact with the World Bank in the preparation for this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. These are the officials from the state federation and also Serb republic government which we were -- that we were meeting throughout the preparation of that report, and so these are the names, Mr. Gotovusa, Mr. Tomic, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Piljak, Belanger [phoen], and as you can see, also, as a part of the World Bank team there is my name according to the alphabetic order. But these are the people that we were meeting in 1994, 1995, and 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And let me go back to one of my earlier questions, which was in 1994, 1995, 1996 when you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina and you were involved in preparing this particular report among with others, did you personally draw any conclusions as far as, say, the Federation was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cvikl. Your Honour, we're going to object to any testimony that goes outside the confines of the expert report that's been submitted, and I don't know whether the witness is going to do that, but it seems to me that counsel is asking for testimony that is not within the bounds of the expert report. I think it's improper. He's here to testify about the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may ask a couple of background questions, Your Honour, and then if Mr. Stringer still wishes to object, then I'll respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the context, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvikl, you wrote this report, and as I understand at some point you were asked to draw some comparisons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you also -- we can see towards the end of your report that you have a whole section on the conclusions that you reached. Were part of those -- the questions that I'm eliciting right now as far as observations that you made in 1994, 1995, 1996, within the Federation, are they part of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: To a certain extent they are because I have -- of course, in preparing for my report I also used this report, and I was recalling what was happening in the 1994, 1995 period, and of course at that time we have been travelling in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the south. We flew into Split, and then from there we went by cars into Bosnia-Herzegovina, into the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and actually, first meetings could not even take place in Sarajevo. They took place in the region of -- around Mostar in Medjugorje, and there I could identify and I've seen a kind of very vibrant economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right here before we get too far ahead of ourselves. The report you cited, you know, in helping your report, which -- we're speaking about 1D 02967, Bosnia-Herzegovina Towards Economic Recovery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the observations that you -- that I was eliciting from you, are they contained in this report which is cited, which is cited as one of the references to your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: No. The analysis which I make for -- you know, in preparation of this analysis of the economic measures, we were not during the 1995, 1994, 1996 period going into very detailed analysis of what is happening in a different part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina because our purpose at that time was of a different nature. We, of course, need to identify whether the Bosnia-Herzegovina as such is sustainable, so that once the World Bank would have again the financial relation with this very country, we would make sure, we would be sure that, you know, both the debts and the new loans that might be lent would be -- the country would be able to pay back. So in that period, we were not going into a very detailed analysis of the environment which was in different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. But the questions that I'm asking you now, do you know whether to any extent you commented on them in your particular report, that is, what you found in Bosnia-Herzegovina when you arrived there as part of the World Bank mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: When, of course, we were as a part of the World Bank mission, there were the World Bank mission, and at the time there was also the IMF mission. The International Monetary Fund was more focusing on the macroeconomic issues while we were focusing more on the ability of the country to somehow, you know, have a vibrant economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But Mr. Cvikl, I would kindly ask you to listen to my question and try to be as precise as you can. For instance, if you were to look at the conclusionary part of your report where you do make references; for instance, if you would look on page 188, final remarks on the economic and social development situation at the end of the war, 1994, 1996. Okay. So that would -- and then you have the following page, the situation in 1995 on page 190, you have a table that you're referring to. You speak of the Muslim majority area, the Croat majority area. So my question is, rather, very precise. When I'm asking you questions about what you observed and what you saw on conclusions that you drew from your personal experience in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994, are they included into your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, they are certainly included in the report based on the information which has been provided to me at that time, which we identified in the World Bank report and also in the IMF recent economic developments report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if Mr. Stringer still wishes to object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I have a follow-up question to put to you. I was looking at the report to be found in Exhibit 1D 0967. That is the World Bank report on the economic recovery in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, this report, I understand that you were involved in drawing up this report. Were there many such experts drawing up this report, or is this report the result of your own personal work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This report has been prepared by a team of the World Bank economists. I was a member of the team, and as in all World Bank reports, such reports are then approved by the, you know, bosses of that team, and that is stated on Roman VII of that very report. At that time, this was Mr. Miseno [phoen] and Kristin Walik [phoen]. But I was part of the team, and I was the first World Bank economist for Bosnia-Herzegovina. So in 1994 and early 1995, I was then the one that was collecting the most information. Once we were preparing the report and we had meetings with a group of officials, there were also other colleagues working along me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. To your knowledge, this World Bank report on the economic situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina drawn up, it would appear published in June 1996. To your knowledge, were there other reports coming from other institutions, for example, the European community or other countries; or to your knowledge, is it the only exhaustive report on the economic situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to the World Bank country study published in June 1996, and that is usually done after, you know, the report is utilized in the internal work of the World Bank, the very important other document is the IMF report, Recent Economic Developments, which has been also cited as part of my -- as part of my report. In the report, in my report, I cite that under the footnote 1 on page -- on page Roman (vii), and that is the recent economic development report, and that is the document 1D 02959. That is the other very important or, you know, really available report, IMF staff country report, recent economic developments number 96 over 104. And the team that was preparing the IMF report and the team that was preparing the World Bank report worked together very extensively, and we have also worked closely with European Union institution, especially the representative of the European Commission, mainly during the time of the preparation for the first international donor conference in February 1996, but I'm not aware whether, you know, at that time -- because Bosnia-Herzegovina was not even negotiating or being close to become the member of the European Union whether there was any other such report prepared by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand well, the IMF report and the World Bank reports are reports in -- back in 1996 are report that we can describe as objective reports because they were drafted by world-renowned organisations and which are the subject of major consideration in international economic circles; and therefore, if I understand well, these two reports are indeed marked by objectivity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you. These are objective reports; they are prepared by, you know, two international financial institutions for a very clear purposes; and they followed scrutiny and a good economy's work that, of course, is known for these two institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. It seemed to me important to specify that. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, going back to my original question, when you went into Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994 to 1996, did you draw any conclusions based on what you saw as a result of your work.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: I was part of the team, and we present these conclusions in that very report, and we have of course seen that the way, especially the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, is organised, the way its prepared would enable us as the World Bank to go ahead with both the membership and providing loans for, you know, taking care of the post-war reconstruction issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next slide --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next slide, which is slide number 4, just very quickly, you already spoke about the methodology to some extent in one of your initial answers to one of the initial questions, and sorry, I just want to focus a little bit on the structure of the report. In looking at this slide, we see that you begin with the background chapter on Yugoslav decentralisation. Perhaps you can explain why it was necessary to start there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, for understanding both by economists and non-economists what was happening in Yugoslavia, especially in the '70s and '80s, it is very important to present what were the kind of overall framework in former Yugoslavia. And the very important feature of Yugoslavia was it was extremely decentralised country, and that is of course is best seen by very decentralised fiscal system wherein actually many small points at the level of local communities major decisions on state and social expenditures are made in a form of a very special para-fiscal funds. So in order, you know, to present and to somehow analyse what was happening later on in 1991, 1994 period on the territory, I analysed and I presented to the analysis of at that time Yugoslav constitution and organisation the way it was done what had been happening on the fiscal and on the monetary front. And that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go step by step. So let's go on to the next slide, and that would be slide number 5. And over here, and the reason I want to go to this particular slide is before we go into any great detail of the report, starting with the former Yugoslav system, as far as your particular report is concerned for what you did in this particular case, having looked at the documents, analysed them, met with individuals, and what have you, did you draw any conclusions? And if so, can you please briefly discuss them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. This main conclusions are presented in this -- my presentation on page 5. What was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what was happening the last years of Yugoslavia when still existed was that there was a very independent economic policy making in individual republics, and unfortunately, reforms that have started in the second half of 1980s and somehow were concluded with the Markovic reforms in the early 1990, they were not successful. These reforms were at that time linked with an attempt of the European Union to invite still-Yugoslavia to become the member of European Union. Yugoslavia had a -- kind of a European agreement at the same time as Austria and Finland had it. Five years later in 1995 Finland and Austria become the member of the European Union, Yugoslavia ceased to exist. What we have seen, and I was observing that from my post at the time in Slovenia, we have seen that there was derogation of old Federation because economically, the old Federation was simply not sustainable, and we could not agree in old environment who will cover the fiscal burden of the necessary reforms that would have to be undertaken in the enterprise and in the banking sector. So the war erupted once Slovenia and once Croatia or Republic of Croatia become independent. Why we went into independence is now already history, but mainly, main point was that we did not want to be in a convoy of six republics slowly becoming member of European Union. Now, what have I seen then, you know, from -- on the basis of the documents provided to me and analysis is that in Bosnia-Herzegovina the situation was, of course, extremely difficult. We have seen that the war resulted into practically immediately 70 percent of the territory being occupied by aggressor authorities. Authorities, the central government authorities in-Sarajevo have not undertaken those economic independence measures that we have done in Slovenia. They have not, you know, issued new currency, they have not undertaken necessary fiscal measures, and there was suddenly a situation that at the level of local communities there were no funds available for the provision of normal state and social services, like, you know, name it: electricity, garbage collection, schools, hospitals, et cetera. So in this very circumstances, local communities started to act, and from the report I've seen that they have started to act in a very similar manner, whether that was Tuzla region or that was Jablanica region or that was Siroki Brijeg area or that was Mostar, or that was actually a very similar manner, also, I've seen over the weekend, also, in Zenica. Now, why local authorities had to act? In Yugoslav constitution, we have a very strong role of local community, the so-called Opstina. They had to act in order to increase supply of goods and services for the benefit of the citizens. And on the other side they have to act, that's what the economists say, in war circumstances on a demand side. So local communities acting and looks like, as there was, you know, almost 100 small economists appearing because in Bosnia-Herzegovina there is a hundred local communities, I have not been looking to the Republika Srpska area, so I can't say what is happening there, but I was looking what was happening in an area within Bosniaks or Muslim majority or in the areas with a Croat majority. And there were actions which resulted in almost, you know, dozens, 20, 30, 40, 50 small economies appearing all over the place. Later on, when that was -- that was resulted, authorities, both the central government authorities and regional authorities, realised that there is a need for coordination, need for coordination in order to assure, as we economists say, economy of scale. Local communities were of a different -- were of a different economic situation, those local communities that they were able to arrest some of fiscal revenues because they were on the -- on a border or because they were able to arrest some of the revenues because they were able to get some funds from abroad from their gastarbeiters, guest workers working abroad, they were in a better situation. But they were local authorities, local communities which they could not perform the government, social and state services, so there was a need for the regional coordination. And that need was actually recognised by the presidency of, at that time, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which issued a decree on districts, where somehow gave up and say, okay, if I can't really control and make sure what is happening in the local communities, let me organise, let us organise seven districts, and let those seven districts coordinate local communities. Now, in 1990, 1991, 1994 period, the economic developments in -- on the free territory, because, you know, once the war or the military activities were concluded, on that free territories local communities and later regional local authorities and later regional authorities started to organise economic life for the benefit of the citizens. Just in the last stage, in the 1993, 1994 period, one could see that they were starting to utilize a normal or a modern government tools; there were budgets being prepared, the financial sector became active, the banking sector, insurance; and thus, they were enabling a normalisation of economic situation. And as I conclude on that slide, when we arrived in the -- early 1995 into Bosnia and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was already up and running, all that was - I can see that now - based on the initiatives and legislation that had been prepared in the period before 1994, 1995. And thus, I conclude that what happened in the period 1991, 1994 was a reaction of local communities in a very decentralised environment to take over functions of authorities to take care for the benefits of the citizens, first on the supply, taking sure about the demand, and thus provide a normal economic development that authorities are usually asked to do in any economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And based on your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. You said a lot of things, and your answer is very relevant in respect of many factors. I'm particularly interested in the part played by local communities. That is item 5 in your conclusion. You explain to us that Yugoslavia was basically operating as a decentralised community, hence, the possible relevance of local communities. You are an economist and you know as such better than anyone that there's always a connection between the political and the economic spheres. Sometimes the political part is going to instrumentalise the economy, or at times it is the economy that is the driving factor for the political realm. But in this case, in which we have to assess the part played by local communities, would your conclusions say that in the 1991 to 1993 or 1994 period in Bosnia and Herzegovina the economic system was solely dependent on local economies or communities, and that as such, the "state," inverted commas, that is, the "state" in Sarajevo was basically non-existent, and that in the end the economic activity was only based on local communities and that the local communities through their economic development were the ones that basically made policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say like this: With the war and because of the lack of actions by the central government authorities, and I have mentioned already before two of them, one was lack of new currency and the second was not very clear reforms needed to kind of surround -- or around the economy. The local -- the central government authorities were landlocked in Sarajevo. They were issuing some decrees. We would maybe later mention some of them, but I have not seen them acting in a very similar manner as we have done in Slovenia. In 1991 when we became independent, we in order to make economy of Slovenia also sustainable, we centralised some of the functions. In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were not able to do that for obvious reason of the war. So suddenly, there was a situation that at the level of the local community, there were government needs that have to be -- or government services that have to be provided to the citizens, but there were no funding provided from the central government. So local authorities had to act, and they have started to, you know, invent new fiscal instruments to collect revenues, so that they will be able to cover the needs of population. That's what I've seen in Tuzla. That's what I've seen in Siroki Brijeg. That's what I've seen in Prozor. They went ahead with a lot of new fiscal measures, collecting revenues to be able to take care of the citizens and also, you know, to ensure what was also their constitutional right to provide logistic support to the defence. So big state companies or socially owned companies at that time ceased to operate. There were no energy. There were no banking sector active. There were no telecommunications lines. So practically all major companies closed their businesses, and the way this country economically survived is that the private sector in -- at the level of the local communities provided not just new employment but provided first, you know, through the trade sufficient -- sufficient amount of food. Provided, you know, together with the donors' assistance, then refugees, displaced people, or people that actually stayed in various territory would have something to eat. I have also seen that especially in the second half of 1992 when the kids were to return to the school year, it was, you know, by the local communities and the regional authorities that they provided funds needed for the re-opening of the schools that were closed over the summer. So you have situation where mainly local communities were those that took the role that was before provided by central government or institutions that were at that time formerly responsible for undertaking financing of government state and social services to the citizens at large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question after this very long answer. As far as you can see, those heading the local communities, especially in the financial economic sectors, were they competent, or was it just goodwill on their part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as an economist, I would say that they actually invented very new tools, how to, you know, find fiscal revenues. They were very -- actually, very similar tools. So in that context, I would say that yes, they were competent. The local communities, they were before the independence responsible for at least organising some of the, you know, government functions, so they knew what was happening. And also, when I was discussing with some of them, I got the feeling that they knew what they were doing but, of course, they had a very limited -- limited amount of the available resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, and I know we'll get to it later on, but you said that there was no money -- no currency that was -- new currency that was issued by Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now at what point -- are you suggesting that at no time Bosnia-Herzegovina issued new currency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: No. I'm not suggesting that, but I'm only suggesting that there was a delay. What was the problem with this delay, when Slovenia and Croatia became independent, in Slovenia and in Croatia a new currency were issued, and this new currency replaced Yugoslav dinar that was before used a cash in Slovenia and Croatia. And that Yugoslav dinars were now, you know, of course moved physically to a much smaller economy. Since in Bosnia-Herzegovina they have not replaced Yugoslav dinar with the new currency immediately, the effect of that was that too much money was chasing too little goods. So the supply of money and available goods was simply too high, and that's why they have immediately very high inflation. Very high inflation means that nobody trusted Yugoslav currency. Later on, the Yugoslav currency was replaced by the Bosnian dinar, but there were too much of that dinars printed, and so as a result of that parallel currency, Deutschemark and others were put in place in order to ensure that you would have some kind of an objective unit of measure, how much, you know, a kilo of bread or a kilo of sugar is worth in currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to follow up on that, in 1994 when you -- 1995 when you first went into Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't know whether it was pre- or post-Dayton, was the Bosnian dinar at that point in time, at that point in time, was it considered hard currency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: No. At that time, we went -- when we went into Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have to take with us cash, Deutschemarks in order to pay bills and, you know, practically in Sarajevo and the Hotel Bosnia, all the pricing was in Deutschemark, nobody was really believing that the Bosnia dinar was there as a kind of a currency that one trusts. It was not a convertible currency, and so that's what we were using. Only later when the convertible marker was established, because it was obviously backed by also international financial institutions, that was the money that we have started to trust, and we started to use that money. But we foreigners were using Deutschemark. I guess others were using dollars, but, you know, I know that in Washington we had problems getting enough Deutschemark to travel into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me back up a little bit. I know we're getting ahead of ourselves a little bit, but you indicated at some point there was a convertible mark and that the internationals were backing it up. Can you briefly describe to us based on what you were able to observe and through your analysis, to what extent, to what extent was the Bosnian dinar backed up by anything in 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: I think it was not backed. I mean, Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have at that time net international reserves. Also, other country not have it, and so the amount of the money printed resulted into a very high inflation, or a very high inflation was the result of the fact that, you know, very huge amounts of the Bosnian dinars were printed, and that's why it was not backed. It was not convertible currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Lets move on now. If we go on to the next slide, and now let's start with your report. This is one of the first items that you speak of, and the number of the slide is 6, which deals with the characteristics of former Yugoslavia. If you could very briefly discuss it. I know that you have touched upon it a little bit but just very briefly so we can move along to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, on slide 6 there are the characteristics of former Yugoslavia, explains what was the responsibility of the Federation and republics and then the role of local communities. Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is a federal state, a very loose federation. Actually, at the level of the Federation there was monetary policy around; there was Yugoslav dinar. However, even that Yugoslav dinar was printed to the amounts as defined within the system of national banks of republics and autonomous provinces. That is very important because later on when Markovic reform actually did not succeed, that was because one of the republics printed too much money. Second, of course, Federation was responsible for setting up the exchange rate, foreign affairs and the really strongest power of the level of the Federation was Yugoslavia military force, both the army itself and the military production which was very much centralised. I was at that time working for the National Bank of Slovenia, and there was a special war service of the National Bank of Yugoslavia responsible for financing this military production. Republics were throughout the developments of Yugoslavia from '50s into '60s and then with constitution of 1971, '74, responsible for most of the issues but in a very peculiar manner. We did not have at the level of republics, governments. We have only so-called executive counsels with Secretariats for particular issues. So there was a Secretariat for education, but major education matters were actually dealt at the level of local communities because local communities were responsible to implement republican policies at the local level. And the way that was done, if you can move to slide number 7, the way that was done was done with a very peculiar fiscal decentralisation where we have had at the level of local communities in former Yugoslavia. In former Yugoslavia, there were, you know, six republics. On average, there were, you know, altogether some 600 local communities. In each of these local communities, you have for a particular government service, and I'll give an example, education. For elementary education organisation in a particular Opstina, you created a special Self-Management Interest Community which composed of two chambers. There was one chamber of teachers that were providing services of education, and then there was a chamber of representative of parents buying services from teachers. And in that very chambers, the decision was made on the level of the money that a particular local community should spend for education. When you have high-level education, a group of local communities formed Self-Management Interest Community for high-level education of particular area; where you have university, in Slovenia, for example, we have two university, so we have just one Self-Management Interest Community to finance university at the level of Slovenia. Now, this system of self-management or the system of Self-Management Interest Community was not just for the social services; it was also for the financing of infrastructure. So for water management, for energy, for, let's say, traffic, roads and railways, there were special self-management interest funds established that collected from enterprises that needed, let's say, services of energy, funds were investment, they also charge energy prices back to those enterprises and thus create an environment into which energy sector has been developed. Now, the problem with this fact is that when you have so many local communities and you have so many self-management interest communities, at more than 5.000 points in the former Federation, decisions on who is using government cash has been made. And that's why Yugoslavia was not sustainable. That's why we had from year to year higher and higher inflation resulting in hyperinflation in 1989. And that's why we say that despite that fact that Yugoslavia, as said on the top of the slide 7, was different than other socialist economy, we replaced the central planning with this self-management system or self-controlled system in early 1950s, it was not economically sustainable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you right here. Before we go on to the next slide, as I understand it you wanted to draw our attention to 1D 02976. That is the constitution of the former Yugoslavia, and you wanted to draw our attention, I believe, to Article 51; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just look at it real quickly. And perhaps tell us, why is it relevant to the discussion that we're having right now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, this Article 51 is relevant because it define the basis -- this is the constitution of Yugoslavia from 1974, how self-management communities interest shall be formed in order to satisfy the personal and common needs and interest at the level of communities. And actually, that self-managing communities of interest, the way they were organised is they were a very peculiar affect or a very peculiar organisation of how fiscal decentralisation has been implemented in Yugoslavia. At the same time, creation of those self-managing communities of interest at the level of local communities were given ability to local communities to take care of a lot of government and social and state services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My apologies. I take it you heard that admonition?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good. Now, why is that important for our discussion here today, for your report? Why is it important?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, it is important for two reasons. First, to understand why the country collapsed. But I think it's more important to -- also to understand that once in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina central government authorities were not really a factor. There was a knowledge, there was experience at the local communities and also the responsibility of local communities to take care of assuring that the common social needs of the population are to be organised in an appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if there's nothing else with respect to slide 7, we can move to slide 8; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So moving to slide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. I do have a follow-up question because you are dealing with essential problems to understand a lot of facts in this case as I understand it, because the three judges in front of you do have knowledge as they have acquired it in the last few years, but you are now dealing with difficult economic concepts, so it's good to specify things and seek clarification. If a western judge looks at the former Yugoslavia, he may think that Yugoslavia had a centralised communist system, but you have just told us that in the '50s, in 1950, in the former Yugoslavia there was a reform that sort of tended to establish self-management, and from that point onwards it was a self-managed country, and there was an increased part played by local communities. Would this mean that the central authority in a system of economic self-management is less powerful, is less strong than in a centralised system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you. Certainly, since in Yugoslavia after the break-up with Stalin in 1948 decided to replace central planning reform with this, what is called, self-management or self-controlled system, the central authorities were throughout economic and political reforms losing their power. I would argue as a Slovenian that that was also due to the fact that there were, you know, forces in Yugoslavia by which republics and local communities need to have this power because it was not impossible in the Yugoslav context to have just unitarian state seated in Belgrade. So central planning -- the replacement of central planning system was a kind of a response of, actually, at that time Tito and the leaders to ensure that Yugoslavia would sustain, and at the same time it was also, you know, ensuring that this economic system would survive. Why was that important? We immediately after the Second World War of course abandoned the central planning because we wanted to have a nominal monetary economy. I give you an example. Already in 1956, in Yugoslavia we have commercial banks established. In case of Poland, the commercial banks were established 30 years later. I believe the similar was also in Hungary, only 1986. The commercial banks where you could deposit money and you could, you know, borrow, were established very early in former Yugoslavia, and actually, the World Bank and the IMF were providing funds to Yugoslavia already in '60s and '70s. So the system somehow enabled activation of the factors of productivity of the labour under the capita that we have through that system of self-management. Was it sustainable over the long term? No, it was not. And that's also -- you know, it's known in theory of economy that this is a so-called concept of the Illiryan firm that there is an intrinsic conflict in a self-management enterprise between the workers that control through the workers' council, the directors, and the directors that of course have to pay back either the credit to the bank or, you know, profit to the, you know, owners. So over the long term, the system was not sustainable. But nevertheless, Yugoslavia was especially in '60s and '70s, you know, economy that was growing mainly based on the foreign borrowing which ceased to exist at the end of 1997. So then in the 1980s, we went into a crisis, but the system is different. The central planning system of the Soviet type and the Yugoslav self-management system is different. We called it market socialism. It's a kind of a very tough word, but the market forces were out there to be assisted. And I will maybe conclude with another example why that happened in 1948. In central planning system, you have also the land being owned by state. We tried to do that. The country became hungry [Realtime translation read in error, "Hungary"]. There was a starve -- you know, people started to starve. So the fact that in the former Yugoslavia agriculture reform taking away the land from the farmers did not succeed and the farmers were able to have 10 hectares of land under their management, and the workers' council systems in the enterprise sectors, that was the basis for a different type of the socialism that we have had in Yugoslavia compared to Soviet Union or -- yeah, compared to Soviet Union or other western -- sorry, eastern European countries. And in that context, you know, reforms that were done in '80s and especially after the Berlin Wall collapsed undertaken, there were, of course, easier -- unfortunately, they resulted in the collapse of the country due to the different views how the country shall be managed, unitarian or the confederation approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this very interesting answer. The time has come for the break. We have to stop for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before bringing in the witness, I'd like to read an oral decision concerning the coming of a witness next week, and I must read it now. Oral decision concerning the information note presented by Petkovic Defence on the 15th of December, 2008. The 15th of December, 2008, the Petkovic Defence filed a notice informing the Trial Chamber of its intention to use four hours to cross-examine the expert witness Davor Marijan [phoen] who will appear from the 19th to the 22nd of January next. In this notice, the Petkovic Defence takes due note of the Trial Chamber's decision of the 11th of December, 2008, through which it is authorised to cross-examine the witness for one hour and 30 minutes. The Petkovic Defence sets out, however, that it nevertheless plans to use an additional two hours and 30 minutes to cross-examine the said witness and that this additional time will be deducted from the overall time allowed for presenting its case. Although this is a notice by way of information, the Trial Chamber decides proprio motu to form a view on this notice with -- by virtue of its power and its duties to control the arrangements for examining the witnesses and presenting the elements of proof. The Trial Chamber recalls, first of all, that through its decision of the 11th of December, 2008, it inter alia rejected the request of the accused Petkovic requesting an allocation of four hours in order to cross-examine the expert witness Davor Marijan stating that this request was excessive. The Trial Chamber, however, decided that one hour and 30 minutes would be sufficient in this instance to allow the Petkovic Defence to complete its cross-examination. The Trial Chamber notes that the Petkovic Defence did not appeal to the decision of the 11th of December, 2008. The Trial Chamber next recalls that the decision of the 24th of April, 2008, concerning the adoption of guide-lines for presenting the Defence elements of proof sets out in its paragraphs 13 to 17 very specific rules regarding the allocation of time available for examining and cross-examining witnesses. According to this decision, the Defence counsel conducting the cross-examination altogether have 50 percent of the allotted time for the examination-in-chief. In this instance, the allocation of an additional two hours and 30 minutes to the Petkovic Defence to cross-examine the expert witness would in fact allow one single Defence team to benefit from time equivalent to that allocated to the Stojic Defence that will examine the said witness, that is four hours. Not only would such a time allocation be in total contradiction with the role set out in the decision of the 24th of April, 2008, but furthermore, would substantially modify the hearing timetable of the Stojic Defence, which is not acceptable. For these same reasons, the fact that the Petkovic Defence informs the Trial Chamber of its intention to allocate this additional time to its own time for presenting its evidence is not likely to sway the position of the Trial Chamber on this point. Indeed, to automatically allow parties to benefit from substantial additional time by claiming that this would be deducted from the overall time allowed for presenting their own case would in fact allow the hearings to continue indefinitely in the Trial Chamber and would countervene the rights of the accused to a swift and expeditious trial. Consequently, the Trial Chamber decides proprio motu not to authorize the Petkovic Defence to use an additional two and a half hours to cross-examine the witness Davor Marijan. The Petkovic Defence will therefore have to conduct the cross-examination of the witness Davor Marijan in one hour and 30 minutes. If need be, the Petkovic Defence may call the witness to appear as part of presenting its own case if it requests the addition of this witness to its list 65 ter and if it accompanies its request with the information required under Article 65 ter (g) of the rule. So in a word, the Petkovic Defence will have one hour and 30 minutes, but if the Petkovic Defence insists on using its 2 hours 30 minutes to question the witness, it will convene him in due course by requesting the addition of the witness to the list 65 ter. There's no problem. We will now bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we are bringing in the witness, on another matter, we filed a supplemental to Dr. Jadranko Prlic's statement that was a response to the Tomljanovich report, as he had indicated in his opening statement that he was planning on doing that, and it was rather extensive. Mr. Stojic objects to it for various reasons, and the Prosecution has objected to it. Even though Mr. Stojic does not cite any authority other the rule itself making a public policy argument, the Prosecution does cite some authority. We would like to have the opportunity to file a single reply, and we would appreciate it if we could have until, say, Monday to file that reply. It shouldn't be more than four or five pages long, but we think that it would be necessary to file that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be authorised reply, four to five pages, by Monday. I will consult with my fellow judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good, Mr. Karnavas. The Chamber accedes to your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please proceed with the examination of your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, before we go on to the next line, there was one particular term which baffled some of the translators and perhaps the court reporter when you indicated for instance there was this conflict between management and the workers, and you used a particular term or theory. If you could kindly tell us again what it is, and go slowly so we can get it down properly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. In the economic theory is a known firm, so-called Illiryan firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Illiryan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Illiryan firm or Illiryan company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That's all we need for now. Thank you, and if we need the spelling of that, we'll get that later on. All right. I believe we were on slide 7, and we can move on to slide 8 at this point unless I'm mistaken, and if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I interrupt, Mr. Karnavas, but the decisive word does not figure in the transcript, the Illiryan. Maybe it would be better to spell it out right away; otherwise, it looks really a bit Kafkaesque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That term didn't come to mind, but I take the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could spell it out for us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, it is spelled I-L-L-I-R-Y-A-N, like Illirya area of what used to be, you know, Dalmatia and the known part. It's a concept which is known between the economists that you want to have enterprise sector, where workers and owners share the responsibility over the management of the company and over the fruit that the company produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we appreciate that bringing the translators bringing it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we can go on to slide number 8, and continuing on with a role of local communities very briefly, if you haven't finished, if you perhaps comment briefly on that, and as I understand you wanted to bring our attention to two particular documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to refer in that very slide is this first notion that while there was a social ownership in Yugoslavia, where there was a general opinion that material resources belonged to the population collectively, one should note that in the case of enterprise sectors, the workers were authorised to manage assets in this very company as long as they were producing positive results. There was a possibility in the Yugoslav system, and here I would like to refer to the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, 1D 02976, Article 130. Where there was a possibility that in the case if workers in an enterprise were not producing positive results, they were producing losses, there was a possibility that the local communities had a right to abolish the self-management rights of those workers and thus preserve for the benefit of the society at large the social ownership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yeah, I can give such an example. It's actually known in Slovenia. It has been known, also, in other parts of Yugoslavia. In Slovenia, we have a producer of wide goods. It's called Gorenje. It is like Phillips of Slovenia. This company in 1985 got into quite big troubles because it was borrowing extensively, it tried to buy a company in Germany, so it starts to create losses. Because of that, the company would not be able to borrow any more from the banks, and the company would go bankrupt. However, a local community of Velenje, Velenje is a town where this Gorenje from Velenje, Gorenje factory resides, has abolished the self-management rights of the workers and appointed a general manager as a caretaker of that very company, and that is what the Article 130 of the Yugoslavia constitution allowed to do it. By this, over the two years with abolished self-management rights of the workers, the new general manager got company again into the positive figures, and today, Gorenje Velenje, which was in the 1985 under the brink of bankruptcy, is one of the biggest Slovenia exporter producing more than 1 billion Euro worth of wide goods and exporting it throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I understand you also wanted to refer our attention to 1D 02974. If you could briefly describe what is in this document. I do note that it has been cited by you in your report.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is the document which I also have, of course, a book of. This is a chapter from the book, which was published in 2004, and that is the chapter written by Mr. Gligorou, and on page 16 of that book, which is in the document, there's an explanation that there was -- there was a different concept of ownership in Yugoslavia than the state ownership. We did not have a state ownership. We had a social ownership, and then in this very article, the author Mr. Gligorou described what was happening in the time of the, you know, reforms in Yugoslavia in the last year of its existence and later in Slovenia as far as the ownership is concerned. The social ownership was two reforms becoming a private ownership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I see here, it was published by the World Bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- the book is "Slovenia: From Yugoslavia to the European Union." It has been published by the World Bank. There are many different authors. I also wrote a chapter on the fiscal issues, and it explains not just the collapse of Yugoslavia in economic terms but how one country that came out of Yugoslavia with a set of reforms started an independence, then become a successful member of the European Union. That's why the title of it is "Slovenia: From Yugoslavia to the European Union."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, unless there's anything else on slide 8 -- if there is, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yeah. Why I put this in -- why I dwell on this in the report is that the role of local communities as defined in the Yugoslav constitution and also republic an constitution was very important so that once war in Bosnia-Herzegovina broke out and suddenly local communities did not have, you know, any abilities to get funds from the central government, they had all these powers vested in local communities and as they were able to undertake necessary measures both in the supply and the demand in a particular area of that very local community. So there was this ability of local community which has been, of course, out there, you know, based on the constitution and where they were -- people understood their responsibility to manage rights but not just waiting for the central government to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, to what extent, if any, did the elections -- because we do know at some point there were elections, to what extent if any did these elections impact on this self-management method that was ingrained in the former Yugoslav system?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, I'm writing the report that, of course, up to elections, there were really, let's say, three most important persons in the particular local community. The president of local assembly, the president of executive council, and the president of the local communist party. When in, I believe, in Slovenia in April 1990, I believe in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the late 1991, free elections took place. In each of those local community, a particular political party won.
