So the person who was elected on a free elections as the president of the local assembly or president of the -- or president of the Opstina, president of a local municipality, he was extremely powerful because he has in a decentralised environment instruments, and he has also the political backing got on the free elections to actually do in the name of the society through the powers vested to him in the free elections whatever need to be done to, let's say, in the war circumstances protect the environment or once the war was over and they took necessary measure on the supply and demand side of the economy. So that power was extremely strong and, of course, the free elections helped that power to be strengthened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If there's nothing else for slide number 8, if we could go on to, then, the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, on slide 9, somehow I explain what is on the macroeconomic side really two most important features of Yugoslavia. One is that of course there was a very decentralised fiscal system where you have had a lot of decisions made at the level of local communities or at intercommunal regional level, and they were also different types of taxes at that time in the former Yugoslavia. There are federal taxes, there were republican taxes, but the most important as far as the size and as far as for the benefits of the population were actual special contributions to finance so-called self-management interest funds. People paid as a part of their gross wage contributions to self-management interest communities funds for different government services: education, health, pension, et cetera. The second important feature is this decentralised monetary system, which was really established only in 1974. That system had two main characteristics. One was that there were national banks as a part of the central banking system created in each republic and also in the two autonomous provinces. These central banks were very instrumental, at least in Slovenia, Croatia, also Former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia, during the independence; to a certain extent, also in Bosnia-Herzegovina but with a delay. The second feature was there was a kind of a unified monetary policy, but that policy had to be agreed by the so-called board of governments of the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the record, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the problem with this board of governors of the National Bank of Yugoslavia that it was composed by republican and provincial governors. So a governor of the National Bank of Macedonia was elected in the parliament of Macedonia, but it represented Macedonia at the level of the Federation. And this board of governors which was politically responsible to the republics was actually not able to manage monetary policy in an appropriate framework, and thus, inflation had been created by too much printing of the money through the system of the Yugoslav central bank. It is also known that hyperinflation created in 1989 and then later attempts by Markovic in early 1990, in the first half of 1990, to somehow run better policies were breached by a decision, one of the governors of one of the national banks of republics, actually National Bank of Serbia, republic of -- National Bank of the Socialist Republic of Serbia to issue money to finance some of the expenditures, and then that then created in kind of a major political fight collapse of Markovic reform. So just to conclude, decentralised fiscal and monetary system somehow prevented Yugoslav Federation to be economically sustainable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just one point of clarification because this may come up later on again. Where you say under the decentralised fiscal system, you mentioned the term "para-fiscal" and then "para-budgetary funds." We've seen this term before in this Court, but if you could remind us from an economic point of view, what does para-fiscal mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Okay. In a normal, let's say, western-oriented -- or western market economy, you would have just one place where government expenditures are defined, and that is government budget, usually adopted in the parliament upon proposal of the government. When you have a special budget like health budget, like education budget, like road budget, that are not within the overall central government budget, we call that in theory para-fiscal budgets. And the first step when you want to create a normal macroeconomic environment, that you take control over how much money government spend. So you need to know how much is spent within the budget, and if you have para-fiscal budgets, para-budgetary funds, then of course you have to prevent it. Yugoslav system of self-management interest -- self-management community of interest, the self-management funds was a typical system where in addition to republican or Federation budget, there were more than 6.000, ten in each of 600 local communities, para-fiscal budget, actually preventing the country as a large, would finance only so much, would spend only so much as we created the value in the economy. And that's why, again, economy not sustainable. So this para-budgetary funds or para-fiscal funds are known in the theory, and also when we -- when I was with the World Bank were analysing the public expenditure management issues in particular country, we always look to this situation whether you have outside the budget any expenditures that you can't control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you just to be a little more concise and shorter with your answers so we can go through this material.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that we're about to go on to the next slide, slide number 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, just for clarity's sake. Mr. Cvikl, you have often referred to communities, local communities. Now, we have been told by another witness that one has to distinguish between municipalities and local communities, the latter being subdivisions of municipalities. I wonder, in which sense do you use the term "local communities"? Are you familiar with and actually using that distinction, or is your terminological system a different one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before -- if I may, Your Honour, if I may, because there may be a point of clarification, the term that you're referring to is "commune" as opposed to "communities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there may be -- so if you could give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. Local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you look into the Yugoslav constitution, the English translation of this community is "socio-political community." The term which I use for local community is units which are smaller than the republics, and this is so -- I mean, the Slovene word or the B/C/S, Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, is "Opstinas." "Opstinas." Now, within these Opstinas or local communities, they could be smaller parts, especially of Opstina consist of a, let's say, big town, you have an Opstina or local community of Sarajevo which has smaller pieces of that local community. But I use the term "local community" for lower parts of republics that are defined within the constitution as the socio-political community. That was the old term, and we then later, at least in the World Bank, you know, went with the local community taking out the basic principle that the local community is the one that has an autonomy over the local matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would now draw the conclusion that this refers to what we have been referred to as municipality. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I meant to -- that was on the list of my questions to get a clarification, and I'm glad that we clarified that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at -- we can go to now slide number 10, and I know that with slide number 10 we will at some point look at 11 and 12 because they're connected, but here in this particular slide, you make reference to the Social Accounting Office. We've heard some testimony about this, but perhaps you can comment on this particular slide, and we can then look at some documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. Another very important characteristic of former Yugoslavia that in former Yugoslavia, the most of the economic relation between the enterprises or between the legal entities was done in a cashless manner. Cashless manner mean without actual utilisation of cash, and the way that was done, it was done through Social Accounting Office. If you look on page 11, there is -- the slide 11, there is a picture, how did -- how this Social Accounting Office was actually organised. It was -- it worked as an agency, and all legal entities, enterprises, local communities or municipalities, even republics, para-fiscal funds, all legal entities have an account, gyro account, an account with this agency. Also, banks, commercial banks have accounts with agency. Even the central bank has an account with agency, and then all transactions were done between the accounts in this very agency. The Social Accounting Office was, thus, extremely important institution to ensure that the transfer of funds have been undertaken in the economy. Even more, because in Yugoslavia there was a quite developed fiscal system, social accountants office also acted not just as the payment mechanism but also as a tax collector. So in the evening, a shop, a legal entity brought to a vault of Social Accounting Office its daily proceeds. And there was a calculation made, so much of daily proceeds with so much of shares taxed, and then the Social Accounting Office, the money was collected, put into the vault, but in the general ledger of a company there was a transaction made to the account of the, let's say, republican budget or to the account of the local community budget for the appropriate portion of the sales tax. In the similar manner, when gross wages were paid each month, a company brought a list of the gross wages, and it says, okay, out of these gross wages, net wages are deposited to the accounts of individuals with commercial banks. The portions of the gross wages which were contribution to different para-fiscal funds for education, health, pension et cetera, they were deposited to particular para-fiscal funds. Why is this important? When the war started and telecommunications were down and -- or the social accounting offices were, you know, destroyed, even if there would be some economic activity, a Social Accounting Office was not operational, tax collection could not take place, and that's why it was very important that once, like in Slovenia when we became independent, the control over the Social Accounting Office is to be undertaken if you want to have any continuation of economic activity in a cashless environment, which was a feature of Yugoslavia at that time to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just make sure that I understand correctly by making a simplified example. Let's say Company X employs Worker A, and Worker A has a salary per month of 100. 100 is transferred by the company to the SDK. The SDK then hands over 70 to the worker. 5 go to education fund, 5 go to health, 7 go to defence, and so forth. Is that the way it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly the way it worked. This is exactly what the Social Accounting Office did. It didn't do this just -- did it for all the workers, but if were just one worker, did for one worker. Everything in cashless, and the worker got cash in the bank because the 70 was, as you have said, given to the bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That, of course, gives then a lot of control to the authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does, but -- well, there are two theories why the Social Accounting Office has been created. In the early '50s, people say it was created because while -- political powers wanted to know what is happening in political enterprises. But later in '60s and '70s, when we all, you know, went into a monetary economy, and it was very cumbersome, to carry around cash to establish cheques clearing system as it's known in America or the gyro account system that is known in European environment in the Social Accounting Office, that was very beneficial for the economic developments because nobody wants to carry around cash. And even what is additional function, tax collection, tax collection was a hundred percent. There were problems where, you know, enterprises just wanted to pay net wages and delay the contribution, but that was more an exemption to the system. The sales tax that has been all collected, so in that context the Social Accounting Office and the organised -- the level of the whole Yugoslavia with its local offices was an extremely important part of the decentralised economic and financial system that existed at the time of the eruption of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why to have a control over that was extremely important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, this SDK system, did it apply also to servicemen, to officials, let's say the Mostar university that had to pay a professor from school? So did it have an account with the SDK, and would it transfer a certain amount on that account, and then the SDK would send to the professor' -- the university professor's account his or her salary, so did that apply to all sectors of activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That applies to all legal entities. Exactly. Also, the, let's say, University of Mostar or University of Ljubljana, first, it got in principle funds to be spent from the para-fiscal fund for education. The funds were -- on account of that university, when the professor was to be paid, net wage went to a professor; the contributions for, let's say, teacher's pension went to the pension fund through the SDK. Everything was done through Social Accounting Office. All legal entities have accounts at the Social Accounting Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one last technical question. In such a system, so there was no direct taxation? Did that mean that people would pay taxes, or was it pay as you earn, and was it done by the SDK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, people paid taxes, but there were two -- there were different type of taxes. We did not have at that time value added. We had sales tax. So the sales tax, which was a tax above the value of the good, was paid in the evening when a company -- sorry, when a shop were selling goods brought the daily income into SDK. And so their, you know, net was deposited to the bank, to the account of that shop, and the sales tax was deposited to the central government and to the local government portion. The employees, the employees earn gross wage, but in principle what they were perceiving is that they were getting only net wages. The so-called personal income taxation, the one which is known in market economy, the one which is progressive, has been only imposed much later, and only in very high salaries, there were, you know, some personal income taxation added. So these were the two main instruments. Also, Social Accounting Office to a certain extent also at that time dealt with some of the customs duties. It depends where the customs were actually charged. Just maybe last sentence. The Social Accounting Office was able to tax everything at the source. So it was not like as you have it now in Slovenia or in America where at the end of the year, you make your tax statement. You were actually -- you know, your money was taken away on a monthly basis at each wage being paid out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For illustrative purposes, I believe on slide 12 we can see a -- sort of a different approach, and if you could please first -- if you could look at this slide. First, tell us, where does this come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: I would like to here refer to the document 1D 02972, where we have on page 43, this is a report by the IMF, Republic of Slovenia, financial systems stability assessment in many different issues including end payment system. And on page 43 of that report, there is a summary assessment on what was happening in the reform of the payment system. And if we now turn to page -- to slide 12. On slide 12, you see how does the payment system looks after Social Accounting Office is abolished. You can see that now a private person has an account with the Bank A, and if he wants to pay to a private person which has an account with the Bank B, it pays that via central bank payment system. So no more Social Accounting Office. However, this is what has happened as a reform of that payment system only in 1997, 1998 in Slovenia and also in some other countries, so this is the actual result of the abolishment of the Social Accounting Office. But if you go back to slide 11, the system that existed at the time of the collapse of Yugoslavia and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and elsewhere was the system that all legal entities have accounts with the Social Accounting Office, so if you wanted to have support to the development of the economy, you need recreate, re-establish or have a functioning Social Accounting Office. So I just refer to this, you know, study of the IMF to show the comparison between the two system, but please note that at the time of the war, the system was as presented on slide 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If there are any questions, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we can now move to slide 13.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, on slide 13, I'm presenting what was happening and how the liquidity, how the cash has been provided in the old system, and what, of course, is important, what then happened actually with the war. Now, in the old system, since everybody has an account with SDK, everything was done cashless. But for small transactions that has to be done in cash, like, you know, payments of daily allowances if people travelled or withdrawal of cash from deposits of individuals with commercial banks, for that you need actual liquidity. You need cash. And that cash resided or was basically somehow, you know, safe in the vault of SDK. So the national bank of a particular republic, the National Bank of Slovenia has a vault in Ljubljana, but for the purposes of distributing cash around Slovenia, there were vaults in different towns in the SDK Social Accounting Office premises, which were usually back to back with commercial banks. Now, during the old time, liquidity was thus provided by transfer of cash from the vault of the SDK to either the premises of the SDK or to the vault of the commercial bank and then to the cashiers or the tellers where you withdraw cash if you are a private person. Now, when in Slovenia we became independent, we replaced that Yugoslav dinar in that vault of SDK with new Slovene-printed currency. In the case of -- in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that came with a delay. That's why I say in this slide 13 that new republican authorities if a country became independent should provide this liquidity. If they have not provided liquidity, that means that, of course, you have immediately problem with normal economic environment. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, two things happened. First, there was a delay on the issuance of new currency; and second, once the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued Bosnian dinar, that dinar was issued in the environment of high inflation or the other way around. Since there was so much money created, since there was so much money created, the result was actually oversupply of money, and that's why there was -- there was, of course, high inflation. In these circumstances, parallel currencies such as Deutschemark came to be active again as the mean of exchange as the unit of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I understand with this particular slide you wanted to draw our attention to two particular documents. The first one, I believe, is 1D 02974.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document -- this is the chapter 6 of the book "from Yugoslavia to European Union" when Mr. Rant [phoen] explains in his writing what had to be done to establish monetary sovereignty of a particular country. And I would like to point to the -- his conclusion on page 94 that -- that 97 -- last sentence on page 94, the 1974 constitutional system with its decentralised organisation of the central banking system facilitated the process of established monetary sovereignty enabled Slovenia to more smoothly separate operations of banks and also to undertake steps necessary for independence. This is what has happened in Slovenia. I have not seen to be undertaken at the start of independence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and thus, it was logical that parallel currency such as Deutschemark or other currencies of the countries that you did business with started to appear on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe you also wanted -- is there a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is, but I do not necessarily need to interrupt you. I can put it -- if you have a follow-up, then I don't want to break your rhythm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was going to the next document, but if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Then perhaps -- it's a bit of a bracket question, but it turned up when you spoke of private banks. Apart from SDK, one wonders, what is the function of private banks? Did they function as credit lenders, and did they take monies for savings, and what was the interest of putting monies to the bank rather than having it in the SDK account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, which means before the reforms that started only after independence, these were not private banks. These were banks that actually, legally speaking, they were joint stock companies, but they were owned mainly by enterprise sectors. It was a very peculiar situation. We had commercial banks, which means that they were able to borrow abroad, but the purposes for which they were borrowing were mainly linked with the support of the, you know, what enterprises needed. To have a kind of a classic private banks, that happened only later. Now, these banks, they had deposits. They had in some -- in the last years of the Yugoslav system, they also have, I would say, quite normal interest rates, but those interest rates were mainly result of the fact that people have not trusted those banks the way you have in a normal private bank environment. I would even say that they were to a certain extent, you know, Ponzi schemes there, you know, Madoff case. Why is this important? Because with independence, most of these banks had major problem not just with liquidity but also with solvency, meaning repaying back to the depositors the money deposited there. So the most powerful institution in the old Yugoslavia to ensure a kind of a smooth financial system was SDK. The banks, especially commercial banks, were helpful for the international transactions, and they were helpful in the case when you establish right rules of the regulation to slowly create and generate some savings in the economy. But initially, I would say at the end of 1980s, we have major problems with the banks, and this is really in the bracket: One of the reason why Yugoslavia collapsed is because we could not agree how we will finance losses in the commercial banks. Would that be done at the federal level, republic level or individual banks, but that is more now kind of an economic debate why the country collapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, I do have a very essential question. Generally, when I have questions, I go straight to essential matters because I want us not to waste time, and we shouldn't spread ourselves too thin. If I understand you well, this fundamental part played by the SDK, because you showed us this scheme on slide 12, that is the outcome of the 1997 reform. I'm still talking about 1991, 1992, 1993, and I go straight to Herzegovina. The Prosecution case is that as part of the joint criminal enterprise, the Croats from Herceg-Bosna and possibly also the Croats in Zagreb changed the currency, so moved from the Yugoslav or Sarajevo dinars to Croatian dinars. The Prosecution case is that the monetary unit which was the legal tender was the Croatian dinar whilst we were in Herzegovina which was a part of Bosnia Herzegovina, but with the SDK system, the fact that you could say that from tomorrow on you would have the Croatian dinar as the legal tender, did that change anything to the SDK-based system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from what I understand, authorities in the Herceg-Bosna had not replaced Bosnian dinar with Croatian dinar, but they have allowed in addition to the Bosnian dinar, which remained as a legal tender, also two additional parallel currency. One was Deutschemark, and the other was Croatian dinar, and later, Croatian dinar replaced by Croatian kuna. Why they have done that, or why it was to certain extent logical that this had been done? You were in a situation where the Bosnian dinar had been in an oversupply. I would like to refer to the document 1D 02959. This is the IMF report. Page 26, footnote 36. In that -- in that -- on that page, you could see that in the so-called Bosnian majority area, the inflation was 73 -- 730.000 in 1992. In Croat majority area was 900 in 1992. In Republika Srpska, it was 73.000. Why am I saying this? When you have a situation where the Bosnian dinar was overprinted and there was a high inflation, and as we will later see a lot of things was happening with the exchange rate, and you cannot -- you don't have a trust, people did not trust the Bosnian dinar, the only other possibility is to allow the use of other currencies. Not to abolish the Bosnian dinar, because I haven't seen in the documents that they abolish Bosnian dinar, but they allow that the gyro accounts and the accounts at the SDK would have first the original -- what's called the original account in Bosnian dinar, and then they would add additional two accounts, one is in Deutschemark and the other one in the Croatian dinar, because they were doing trade with Republic of Croatia and they were doing trade with other countries where they were using those two additional parallel currencies. So I'm not -- I'm not seeing this as a breach of the monetary sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I see this as a mean to support the economic developments if you have such high inflation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer is connected to the inflation rates, and then one can understand then one will resort to a currency that will be less susceptible to problems than the Sarajevo-based dinar, and this has not been tackled yet. The SDK is well connected to the central branch, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the SDK is well connected in the central bank in the normal circumstances. But I understand that the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also that is what I was discussing with wise governor and governor of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When we were visiting them in 1994, 1995, they did not have a control over the whole territory because they were -- the SDK offices in Tuzla, they were acting independent of SDK office or the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina office in Sarajevo. In the same manner, I've seen that in Travnik and the same manner, we've seen that in Mostar. So central bank would provide to the vaults, in the normal circumstances, to the vaults of SDK money printed for the purpose of, you know, the currency, but that had not been done. I don't know how much of these funds were really made available throughout that Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the discussion which I had with one of the wise governors of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina was that this, really, control of National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina over the whole territory of the Federation took place only in 1994. But in 1992, 1993, these local communities were their own, and there are a lot of documents which I observed where they are setting up the exchange rates which were, you know, quite different depending on how much money was on a particular territory and what was the level of the goods to kind of balance the supply the demand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling me under oath that back in 1994 you had a conversation with the governor of the central bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he told you that prior to 1994 he had no link or control over the local SDKs? Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Under oath. I had discussion both at that time both with Mr. Omicevic and later on with Mr. Backovic, Endor [phoen] Backovic, I ask him this again, Mr. Backovic, on December 21st last year when I last visited when they actually were able to take over control over the whole territory, and his explanation to me was 1994. Also, when we visited Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994, 1995, we even in the circumstance that there was a control we were still not -- the foreigners were still not using Bosnian dinar because inflation was still very high. So yes, Mr. Omicevic and Mr. Backovic, that's what they were telling us, that they were not able to, you know, control from the monetary point of view the whole territory of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina because I understand that in the area of Republika Srpska, Yugoslav dinar was there up to the replacement of the Yugoslav dinar with convertible mark, which was only in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a small question. 1994 in the area was an eventful year, so it would be interesting for us to know, if it is possible to know, whether your interlocutors referred to a specific moment during that year? Was it in the beginning before May, for instance, or was it towards the end? Maybe you don't know the answer, and I take that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were starting to have discussion with authorities in the fall of 1994. First, in Warsaw they were coming to us. Then in 1995, we came into Bosnia-Herzegovina and we, the foreigners, were not using Bosnian dinar. We found out and we came to, you know, different parts that, you know, Deutschemark was the kind of currency that one need. Once post-Dayton Agreement convertible mark was put in place, at that very time everybody started to use convertible mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I believe in reference to the document that you have been speaking of, which is -- this is document 1D 02959, you brought our attention to footnote -- to paragraph -- to page 26, footnote 36, but I also believe you wanted to draw our attention at some point to a couple of tables, one on page 82 and another one on page 102. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could just look at now page 82 of this document. Perhaps you can describe to us, what are we looking at, keeping in mind that we are under somewhat time constraints.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, on -- page 82 of that document explains -- this is an indices or the physical scope of industrial production, and in column 3 on the top, total industry, there's a figure 8.6. That means that if 1991 is 100, then in 1993 the level of industrial production was at 8.6 percent or what it was in 1991. In 1994, they have a little bit increased up to 9 percent. But a drop of industrial production as a result of the war was 91 percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to page 102, there's another table, and I believe you wanted to draw our attention to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. Page 102 shows the expenditure shares as a percent of total expenditures in Bosniak majority area, and these are the figures for 1994, and if you could see in the line social fund expenditure, we see that there's a quite a major difference between what is the level of expenditures in the Croat majority area, 80.2 percent, and what is in the Bosniak majority area which is 8 percent, which means that in the Croat majority area they were spending more money for the social funds expenditures, and most likely that is a result -- if we also look in the same document, table 29 on page 100, there we can see that in the 1994, the total revenue, the fiscal ability in the Croat majority area is 352 million Deutschemark, one in the Bosnian majority area, only 47.9 million Deutschemark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: And the reason why I'm saying this is because I would like to suggest that we move to slide 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But before we do that, if we look at -- going back to page 102, you pointed out to us the column, the social fund expenditure. If you look at the very first line, wages and contributions for the Bosniak majority, we see zero, whereas the Croat majority we see 11.2, and for Republika Srpska we see 7.8. Does that -- is that relevant in any way, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, also, this is relevant. That means that in the Croat majority area, in addition to paying pensions as explained in this line of social fund expenditures, they were also paying out wages to the employees, while in the Bosnian majority area they were not paying wages and contributions for the government employees. So the fiscal situation in these two areas were very much different, and that's -- if I may suggest, if we move to page 40.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Sorry. Slide 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slide 14. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: When you have a situation -- when there is no liquidity provided by the central bank, when you have a situation -- when you have a dire economic situation, there are really two options that authorities have chosen to solve that problem. One is to print the cash needed. The other is to collect fiscal revenues via different form of taxation. And what I have seen, especially when I look into the war budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for practically 98 percent of the revenues is actually borrowing from the commercial -- from the central bank, which means printing the cash needed, a much logical and much more correct way to manage the economy is to collect fiscal revenues via different forms of taxation. For that, you need tax administration, which means you have to re-establish social accounting offices, and for that you need to go with imposition of different forms of revenues, and that has been done at the level of local community -- either in Croat or in the Muslim areas at the level of local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to just go back one second because I think this may be important because you did indicate now that practically 98 percent of the revenue is actually borrowed from the central bank, which means just printing. Can you please describe, what do you mean by that? Because you talked earlier, and there was a question about confidence level. We talked about this particular currency not having any backing. It now appears that you're telling us something that's a little bit more complete that might give us some -- might be helpful for us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, there is in the Official Gazette of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Official Gazette with war budget. And that war budget in the structure of its revenues, 98 percent of the revenues is money printed from the central bank, and that, of course, when you have such situation, then you have, of course, a very high inflation. While in the level of the local communities, the way they started, since they could not print the money, they started to collect fiscal revenues for different forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it sounds from what you just told us that we have a situation, at least in Sarajevo, that is somewhat similar to Zimbabwe today, where Mugabe is just printing money to finance his government. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, 730.000 high inflation 1992 is a result of authorities printing the money, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if there's nothing else for slide 14, we can move to slide 15.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, the slide 15 and slide 16, they were explanation how one state should operate. When I was looking to all these documents, I of course as an economist need to put a frame, and that frame is best described on slide 16. That is a slide which is a figure 5.2 from the document 1D 02966.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which is? If you could just --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yeah, which is a book, "Managing Public Expenditure," a reference book for transitions country, edited by Richard Allen and Daniel Tommasi, and there on page 153 of that book or on the slide 16, here we -- it explains what do you need to do in a particular state to have a normal management of economy. You need to clearly establish a relation between domestic and external sector. You need to ensure that in the real sector, the one in the middle, the goods and services market, you have appropriate relation between what are known as other domestic sectors. These are the households providing labour and owners providing capital so that you organise economy, and then you need to have a general government collecting taxes for the government to be able to undertake government services, and you need to have a working banking sector that providing financing of all that. If you don't have these all sectors up and running, it is extremely difficult to undertake, of course, normalisation of economic situation. Authorities, the central government authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina have not undertaken all these measures. They have done them with a delay, and for these very reasons, local communities as presented in follow-up slides have done a lot of that measures at the level of their own small economies as defined in their small local communities,

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If there are no questions, Your Honour, we'll move on to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to slide 17.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: On slide 17, we of course claim on the basis of the analysis that while in the same time internationally recognised -- Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same time as Slovenia and Croatia, while it was internationally recognized a sovereign state, it was not an effective state because it had not undertaken measures to ensure its economic viability. As presented in the previous pictures, relations among key economic sectors did not materialise as they should have. Of course, there are obviously reasons why that had happened: military activities, inability of the central government to have a control out of Sarajevo, no taxes, no customs control established, very high portion of the budget for military expenditures, very low level of economic activities. But the fact is that while the war in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina prevented the creation of the institution that they needed, somebody need to act. Authorities haven't done as presented in the bottom part of that slide 17 -- they haven't undertook the customs authority. The central banking authority acted with a delay, Social Accounting Office at the level of the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina was not functional, so they did not have the government -- the tax authority, and government also did not acted as regulator. If you move to slide 18 and then slide 19, the slide 18 is the first of the two slides which explain what was the result of the war. Clearly, more than 70 percent of the territory had been occupied. The government of Republic of Bosnia was not able to establish customs control, no new currency issued, no collection of taxes, and very weak execution of public expenditures management functions, which means creation of the government services. Thus, there was practically a complete collapse of the pre-war economic system. I have seen this reports by the economic departments, and I wanted to check whether that was correct, and of course, when I was looking into this legislation and I was looking for whether they have done all this, I of course was not able to find it, and that's why, of course, we have a situation where a normal pre-war decentralised system was not operational. That was, of course, also due to the fact that telecommunication were down, railways were down, roads were down, and practically there were a standstill at the level of activity of the local communities activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe, Mr. Cvikl, for this particular slide, slide 18, you wanted to draw our attention to P00274 as the first document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the document. It's a translation of the Official Gazette of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where in the preamble under -- on page 1 of the translation, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, in the fifth line, says that is the regressor [sic] who refuses to halt aggression has occupied over 70 percent of the territory, which is -- which was for me proven, of course, that authority could not act and the military activities were a very, you know, strong factor of why that had not been undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see that's as of 20 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Exactly. That is the -- June 1992 when the authorities declared that proclamation of the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe you also wanted to draw our attention to P00128, and I should caution you that when you're away from the mics, it may be giving the folks translating you or interpreting you some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the warning. I will put the paper in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. P00128?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: This is -- P00128, I would like to refer to page 32, section E, the economy, where there is a description of what had happened at the beginning of the war. And it says that: "The beginning of the war and to some extent also before it, the overall former system collapsed completely and all economic activity and payment operations stopped while all communication, railroad and telecommunication links were severed. With the stoppage of economic activities" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Cvikl, because somebody is trying to translate you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Thank you. "With the stoppage of economic activities, all sources of revenues for leaving and the conduct of the war dried up while the need for funds was greater than in peacetime."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything else in this particular document that you want to draw our attention on, or shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So then we can go on to the next slide, and that would be slide 19, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: The slide 19 somehow conclude what was the result of the war. Since the steps and measures required for an independent state were not undertaken, economic system and economy came to a standstill. There was a very limited economic production, and since the tax administration was not established, since the Social Accounting Office at the level of the whole country was not implemented, even this limited activity was not taxed. It is also known that particular fact was at that time the banking system, 1995 when we -- even 1995 came into Bosnia-Herzegovina, the banks were still not operating, at least not in Sarajevo. And thus, collapse payment system did not support even if there was a limited economic activity. And as I've already said, the central bank authority, the monetary authority needed for a kind of sustainable economic system and a revival of economic activity of the whole country was regained much later when convertible mark was issued in the post-Dayton period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to clarify that point, when the convertible mark was issued by the central bank authorities, who was running the central bank authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, it is known that according to the Dayton Agreement it was run by a foreigner, Mr. Peter Nicholl, I believe, from New Zealand or Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. From New Zealand. That's correct. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I would only like to ask one question here, and then I would like to make a small remark. This -- I believe this page 19, the result of war, second of the two of them, then it was mentioned that the steps and measures required of an independent state were not undertaken. And now I would like to ask Mr. Cvikl if he would be able to tell us that, that why the steps and measures were not undertaken on the one hand, and on the other, if he feels that was there any realistic ground to believe that these steps were really to be undertaken in light of his earlier statement when he spoke about the banking systems and the problems that he himself mentioned, that in many instances and mainly in 1992, 1993, the banking system simply could not work because of the situation in a bigger part of the country, I mean Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he mentioned several places like, I believe, Travnik, Mostar and others. So does he believe -- I mean, do you believe, Mr. Cvikl, that there were practical possibilities to take steps and measures required of an independent state, unquote, in that case, or it was only frankly wishful thinking on the part of the central government or on the part of any other entities? It is my question, but being a Hungarian, I listened carefully what you previously said, and since also in Hungary we have followed with great interest the economic and political, financial development of former Yugoslavia at that time. And I have only one remark to make. Earlier today, you referred to the starvation in Hungary, starvation in Hungary. Now, it is not my -- no, I know that it was in the transcript. You refer to the fact that even in Hungary there was starvation. I would like to say - let me finish, Mr. Karnavas - that it is not the national pride which now makes me make this statement, but the -- knowing of the fact that in Hungary during that period of 1948, 1950, et cetera, we did not have starvation. We did have -- since I lived that time, I know we did have some period of starvation in 1945, early 1946, first, because of the German army took whatever they could when they went back to Germany, and number 2, also, because then the Soviet army took whatever was left there by the Germans. So, therefore, I would say that, yes, there was really starvation but not that period of time which you made the reference to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to apologise what was in the transcript because I have said there was starvation in Yugoslavia and people were hungry. People were hungry. That's what I guess is in the -- and, of course, I refer this because I just want to explain how in 1948, people were, of course -- the hunger and starvation in Yugoslavia was prevented by stopping the agriculture reform, stopping taking land from the farmers, and we'd be assured that the farmers continue with the production of the food for the food markets, and thus we had to have the workers' self-management and the workers having the wages to buy that goods, food in the market, and my parents told me how was that in '48. Now, on your question, Your Honour, I have stated on slide 17 and slide 19 that I simply observed that the steps and measures required of independent states were not undertaken. I'm saying that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an internationally recognised state, but it was not an effective state, but people still need to survive. And since we had a decentralised economic system, it was logical that at the local community level, authorities started to act. Sarajevo government, central governments landlocked; they were issuing different type of legislation, not known outside; and then authorities acted, and they acted in a very similar manner as if they would be creating independent states for their own territory. Now, when I say independent states, I mean economic areas that are to work and to deal with other parts. So that's why I've seen in Tuzla creation of the fiscal revenues. I see that in Zenica, Travnik, Mostar. Now, I'm an economist, and I haven't judged whether they were possible to do it, and I have said they could not do that because there was a military aggression. But on the other side, once the military activity, you know, calmed down and the government remained landlocked in Sarajevo, it was logical from the economic point of view and from the -- yeah, from the economic point of view and given the authorities that were vested in the local communities that these authorities acted, first in local communities and later at the level of regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cvikl, for your answer on both issues, and I'm satisfied with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question put by my fellow judge and your answer that was based in particular on tables 17 and 19, allow me to ask you the question that I was burning to ask you but I was waiting for the right moment. In slide 17, you indicate clearly and specifically that internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina that recognised this state internationally seemed, in fact, to raise a number of problems linked to economic factors, and I was very struck by the document where we realised that industrial output on a basis of 100 fell to 8 percent. In other words, there was major economic collapse. Now, my question is as follows: In such a situation, is it logical to recognise a state that doesn't function economically, and to support my question, I'm establishing a parallel with Kosovo. I know that the Slovenian presidency managed the -- issued the recognition of Kosovo, and you as the expert, I would ask you whether from the economic standpoint current that Kosovo presented the same situation as Bosnia-Herzegovina back then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the short answer would be no. There's a difference, and the difference is the following: European Union member states recognized Slovenia, Croatia, and Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the same time. Now, Slovenia and Republic of Croatia have undertaken some of the measures, and as you know, Slovenia was immediately attacked by the Yugoslav Army, and over the two weeks' war we were able to get to some kind of the peace. And here is the answer why there's no -- it's not the same situation in Kosovo now as it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991. For all practical purposes, and I have visited Kosovo as the member of parliament a couple of times, effectively there is a, you know, force out there that, you know, prevent or can prevent eventually military attacks, and that was not the situation in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992. So all the military forces that we drove from Slovenia after the October 15th actually moved south, and since Bosnia-Herzegovina was really the core of the Yugoslav military production, those forces end up in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why this 70-percent possession of the land by non-Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, where in the case of Kosovo it is different. There is a real force out there that could prevent -- you know, EU lacks now police force, et cetera, that could prevent such aggression. Is this economically and from the -- all other issues the smartest decision, I can't comment on that. About Kosovo, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm looking at the clock. It's time for the break. We'll resume at 6 p.m., and Mr. Karnavas will have an hour to continue the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in session, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could go to now slide 20. I believe that's where we left off, and we can go rather quickly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think there might be an open mic on the Bench, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Well, in slide 20 we explain what kind of actions would need to be taken in order to strengthen the economy, to strengthen the tax and revenue authority, re-establish the SDK and for that, one would need to repair the telecommunication networks. And those measures were not implemented. They were implemented to the level of local community, and I have seen some of those measures, region-wide measures, implemented in the area of Herceg-Bosna and to a certain extent from what I've seen, in Tuzla region by a couple of local communities where they were sharing some of the -- mainly approach to the strategic reserves which they have had there. Now, the war resulted into a very difficult situation. And in this situation, authorities which were according to the Yugoslav constitution responsible to manage affairs on their own territory, they had to act. They had to act on supply and on demand side. And from the documents which I have seen, authorities, local authorities have acted in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything else, or should we go on to --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: We can go to slide --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slide 21?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on to slide 21.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: In slide 21, we of course explain why there was a complete collapse of economy, and the main reason was that the enterprise sector ceased to operate. Manpower was called under arms, no energy was there, raw material supply was very limited, and domestic shops were closed. And the reason why society, why people survived were really two reasons: One, the food markets operated throughout the war, which means that the private farmers were providing to the food markets stuff throughout the war; and the private sector initiative took place. There were hundreds of new enterprises established, especially in the trade sector, and this enterprises provided the supply of goods needed for the benefit of the population, and these enterprises and the donor assistance somehow in a situation where we had 91 percent drop of the industrial production, enabled the survivor of the population throughout the war period up to 1991, 1994 period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, with respect to this particular slide, you wanted to draw our attention to 1D 02959?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, this is the -- exactly. This is the report of the IMF where we again show on table 11, page 82, this indices, very low indices of the physical scope of industrial production summarising how bad was the situation, on page 82 of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we saw that already. Then I believe the other document is 1D 02967.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, here, this here I'm referring to the Bosnia-Herzegovina toward economic recovery report by the World Bank, and I would like to refer to page Roman xvii when at the bottom of the second paragraph there is an assessment made by the World Bank team at that time that the external financing requirement need was currently estimated at 5.1 billion dollars for the initial three to four years, and this is big amount, a big amount because compared to the figures which we have seen before, this is almost six to seven times bigger than the amount of the old fiscal revenues for the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just to make sure that everyone sees that, that's on the second paragraph on this particular page, and it's the last sentence of that paragraph, which is titled above it: "Reconstruction: Priorities and Organisation." All right. Now -- and I guess we can go on to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. On slide 22, I'm summarising the monetary policy area. The National Bank of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not implemented immediately the policies needed, and since there was a lack of unique domestic legal tender that people would trust, and as the other currencies, the Deutschemark, Croatian dinar, started to play the role the paralegal tender, and convertible mark was established much, much later, in the meantime, in the meantime, local communities implemented the traditional measures of the central state authority. We have seen later on a situation where local communities were actually undertaking those measures which would be normally done by central banks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you just give us an couple of examples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, just simply a matter of functionality. I believe that under second dot: "The national bank delayed provision of the new currency. The currency was not widely accepted..." So far so good. "...and it was hard currency..." I believe that you should have said that it was not a hard currency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a hard currency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you want to give us some examples or are we going to be seeing some examples later on concerning what was done?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: We will see them later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if we go on to the next slide, which would be 20 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: The slide 23 and slide 24 explains how the war affected the fiscal system. Since we have said that the domestic payment system ceased to operate, Social Accounting Office not being activated, there were no ability for collection of domestic fiscal resources, and thus, para-fiscal funds, the self-managed interest communities that were supposed to provide money for the social services, were not really effective. And thus, initially in practically all local communities, different types of fiscal revenues were implemented, and of course authorities have undertaken this by either obtaining fiscal resources, or in some cases, and that was a very nice case in Tuzla, they even provided food packages as a mean of payment. Instead of giving people a wage, they were giving them a monthly rationing food package as the monthly wage for the services, let's say, of the health officials in a local health facilities in Tuzla. On slide 24 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Cvikl, to speak a little bit slower because as we go into the evening, everybody is getting tired, so if you could slow it down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Thank you. On slide 24, here I summarized what is happening on the expenditure sides. As there were no gross wages, as there were no economic activity, no gross wages, there were no obligatory contributions to be paid into the accounts into the different para-fiscal funds. Thus, health, pension, education and other funds that would finance social and state expenditures did not have resources. Pensions were not paid; health services were not receiving funds through this system via from central authorities; schools, universities stopped receiving funds, and they would continue to be closed, they would continue to not operate unless somebody stepped in. And in that context, I conclude the situation of the war and fiscal system with the last bullet where I say that budget users, different entities being financed from budget, either budget or para-fiscal funds, they became completely dependent on ability of local communities to finance these expenditures. That is result of the war and result of the collapse of the existing decentralised fiscal system and collapse of the economic activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to slide 25, which is your summary, and I believe you wanted to draw our attention, as well, with this particular slide to 1D 02964.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. In this slide, I somehow summarized as an economist what was the overall economic situation. And the best description of this situation is on the document 1D 02964, where the Ljubiski municipality had issued the following communique that the regular supply of electricity was interrupted, and we hereby inform the population that there will be no electricity until further notice. And that's why measures have been undertaken to ensure at least the minimum amount of electricity possible. It's a kind of a very vivid picture that, you know, on April 21st, 1992, the country practically came to a standstill with no electricity being provided, despite the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina has ample ability either in power -- either in thermal power or hydropower to produce electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if you can now -- have you concluded with your summary or shall we ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: We can continue, but, you know, as I say in the last point, since the government of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo was unable to effectively implement the measures, local authorities started to act independently. And as we presented in the follow-up part of the report and in follow-up slides, these occurred in a very similar way, whether that was a Muslim or Croat majority area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so with that, unless there are any questions from the Bench, we could go into more concrete situations with the next slide, which is 26, "Activities of Local Communities."

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. Local communities need to act for two reasons. First, they need to act to defend themselves, but once they defend themselves from the aggressor attacks, they need to restore basic economic conditions. And in that context, as central authorities were not active, local authorities became the key elements for what I call national governance, of the governance of economy in their respective areas. They had for that constitutional mandate. They had the power to act on many issues, and here I would refer to document 1D 02994, which is the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there is on page 91, in chapter 7, Article 262, which explain the responsibility of the municipality being, of course, responsible to ensure the conditions for the work -- for the life and work of the working people and citizens. And in that context, the local authorities acted as, you know, defined in the constitution, but even more, if I refer and I would like to refer to another document, which is the document 1D 0247. Sorry, 2047.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: This is the document issued on August 1st, 1992, by the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopting decree law on the application of the law on the financing of general social needs, and in this very decree law, in Roman ii, section 2, the financing of the functions and tasks of socio-political communities during an imminent threat of war and during a state of war, in Article 2, it is explained what -- which general social needs shall be covered in war or during the war. And that is first the financing of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down a little bit so we can all -- now, this is rather important to absorb.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. Article 2. It starts by defining what are the most -- what are the priority to be finding during an imminent threat of war and during a state -- and it says, first, the financing of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; second, the work of the presidency and other administrative bodies; third, the securing and maintenance of commodity reserves; fourth, additional resources to municipality; and then it continues, five, financial support for families or persons, et cetera. But I would like also to refer on next page to Article 3, defining that all these needs shall be referred -- the needs referred in Article 2 of this decree shall be financed from the budget, and that budget is hereinafter referred to as the war budget. So the decree issued by the presidency has given local authorities or socio-political communities ability to establish war budget. Why is this important? In Article 3, the war budget is defined. In the Article 2, what are the priorities of the needs? And in Article 20, I would like to refer to Article 20, which is under the Roman iii, revenues of the socio-political community. In Article 20, it is defined that during an imminent threat of war and during a state of war, the socio-political community may determine new sources of revenue and abolish the existing ones, et cetera. Which means that here with this decree law, the president was giving the local communities an authority to issue new "legislation" by which they would be collecting new fiscal resources. They would have to put this new fiscal resources in the war budget and finance what is the -- requested from the presidency in that decree, and that is to defend themselves and to, of course, take care of the needs of the population on their own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One minor detail. Article 20, which you've just discussed, and it says, i.e., you know, and it gives some examples, I guess: "Increase, lower and abolish tax rates. Determine tax relief and the exemption of certain taxpayers..." and so on. Are these the sorts of activities that are normally carried out by the state or by the local communities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: These activities are normally activities that are done by the state. State is the one that in the name of the power vested by its constitution issue tax obligation, give to certain taxpayers possibility of exemption. The Presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina realising that they cannot do that, they have transferred that state function down at the level of the municipalities or so-called socio-political communities, of course, and those socio-political communities according to the Bosnian constitution were actually Opstinas or municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we see that that's done in August of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct. And that's why I -- you know, when I was done looking into particular activities, I was not surprised that they were done all this what would be the normal function of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there's anything else or any questions from the Bench, we can move to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's an important article that wasn't cited that follows up on what you were saying, seems to me to be Article 8, that clearly sets out that additional resources may come from the municipalities, which would tend to indicate that when the state is unable through its national budget to meet the budgetary expenditures owing to a war situation, then there is recourse to the local authorities. Would you confirm that Article 8 is indeed consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the Article 8, it says that the war budget shall provide additional resources from the municipality to finance needs. But when I looked into the war budget for 1992, I have not seen on the expenditure side those additional resources being provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If there's nothing else from this particular slide, then we can go on to slide number 27; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if we could go to slide 27.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: In slide 27, I'm explaining what kind of economic measures local communities have undertaken, and I've started it, of course, they have undertaken macroeconomic measures because they were to ensure the balance of the supply and the demand. And the second, they -- as vested by this decree which they just discussed, they established a new fiscal setup. They take over public services that used to be responsibility of the central government, and then I under the last bullet summarized what kind of measures were out there, and there are really four groups of measures: Measures to ensure defence, macroeconomic measures, microeconomic measures, and the measures to ensure government services, and in my report I cite those measures and I group them according to the structure which would -- which economists would usually do and as explained in the last bullet of that slide 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand this with particular slide in keeping with these measures, there are several documents that you wish to go through and point out certain things for our edification. And I believe the first document is 1D 03000, which is cited in your report, of course.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, that is the -- this is the decision by the Ljubuski municipality on establishing a commission that will define the exchange rate of the Yugoslav dinar relative to other currencies as stated in the -- para first, and this would be normally the function of the central bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see that that is on 24 April 1992, rather early on, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the next document is 1D 00786.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes, this is decision by the Jablanica Municipality Crisis Staff. I would like to refer that this is a new document. I am not -- I haven't cited this document in the report. I have got this document over the last weekend in preparing for this, and this is the executive decision of May 13, 1992, to form a working group that would draft documents necessary to overcome problems arising from these functional system of payment transaction and fiscal and monetary policy in Jablanica municipality. That is, again, measures undertaken in Jablanica, one of the local community where they have undertaken the functions of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, which I also believe is a new document which you only saw recently, and that is 1D 02337.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. This is document issued by -- on July 7 by Siroki Brijeg municipality where the control of movement of goods in the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality is defined, and it says in Article number 1 that the control of entry and exit of all goods in the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality will be carried out by the relevant inspection services with mandatory assistance by military and civilian police, which means that this Siroki Brijeg municipality established the control checkpoints to ensure the control of the economic area. And it's a new document, but it's one of these new documents which was given to me over the last weekend but confirms that this is one of the classical macroeconomic measures that the particular economic unity would have to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we go on to the next document, again, a new document, 1D 02523, 1D 02523.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: This is the document, again, by the Siroki Brijeg municipality of October 27, 1992, where the exchange rate are defined, and in Article 3 it says that for payments in German mark, the exchange rate should be set above the exchange rate that had been at that time defined for Deutschemark and Croatian dinar by National Bank of Croatia. And then it says also that for other currency there should be a premium of 5 percent each point above. Again, a measure of local community of Siroki Brijeg that is actually a state -- usually a state measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02984. 1D 02984. Again, this is a new document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document by another municipality. When I started -- when I finished this report, of course, I got a mountain of documents, but when I saw this document over the weekend, it's, again, a document which in Article 2 defined that the single joint tax and contribution rate is defound [sic] in the amount of 80.6 percent of net payment in money and in kind, which means, here they were collecting either fiscal resources in cash or in kind, and then it says that this -- in Article 4, that this joint tax and contribution rate actually is for assuring funds for contribution for healthcare, education, pension, disabled insurance, all functions which were before functions of the central government state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I have a technical question I must raise. Are these documents on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, they are. They were only new for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: New for Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But not for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, not for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm glad that you brought that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, because of course we have rules and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at Article 4, for instance, and you just commented on that, this would be an example, for instance, of what you were speaking earlier about para-funds. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next document, again, this is new to you, this would be 1D 03018.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document of October 26, 1993. Municipality of Travnik in difficult war circumstances of the middle of 1993 had set an agenda, and in this agenda, I would like to refer to two items of agenda. The first, number 3, and then number 6, Current Affairs. Number 3, defining the exchange rate for dinar is done on page 1D 57-0654, explained further, and it defined that in this municipality they have decided what shall be the exchange rate for convertible currencies. And interesting is, of course, that they are somehow defining the cross-exchange rates between Deutschemark and dollars, but, of course, defined that one Deutschemark shall be worth 100.000 Bosnian dinars. And second, what I would like to refer is that current affairs, and that current -- just a second.
